claims.text: A hierarchical nano- to sub-micron grain structure will improve the mechanical performance of refractory high-entropy alloys under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
Additional grain-boundary interfaces will trap and annihilate radiation-induced defects.
Hierarchical grain refinement can improve performance without compromising thermal stability.
Severe plastic deformation can produce the proposed hierarchical grain structure in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Additive manufacturing followed by targeted annealing can produce the proposed hierarchical grain structure.
Heavy-ion irradiation and helium implantation are relevant exposure modes for refractory high-entropy alloys intended for severe nuclear environments.
Hierarchical grain boundaries and interfacial regions act as sinks for irradiation-induced point defects and dislocation loops.
Increasing defect-sink density promotes rapid defect recombination.
Rapid defect recombination reduces irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
The refined hierarchical microstructure enhances mechanical strength and hardness.
The refined microstructure will maintain the alloy's thermal stability and irradiation resistance.
Relative to a homogeneous coarse-grained or uniformly nanocrystalline baseline, the treated alloy will have higher yield strength at high temperature.
Relative to the homogeneous baseline, the treated alloy will have higher ductility at high temperature.
The treated alloy will show irradiation-damage resistance comparable to the homogeneous baseline, including resistance to void or bubble formation.
The proposed effect should persist at reactor-relevant temperatures and fluences if the hierarchical structure remains stable against grain coarsening.
